query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The structural and chemical stability of near‐equiatomic multi‐element nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions is governed by the competition between high-entropy stabilization (which favors a single-phase solid solution) and the enhanced surface-driven kinetic processes (such as differential atomic diffusion and selective oxidation driven by atomic size and redox potential disparities) that promote phase segregation or surface oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, near-equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles (e.g., PtIrOsRhRu or similar compositions) synthesized under conditions that freeze in a high-entropy and homogeneous distribution.
generation.intervention: Expose batches of these nanoparticles to controlled high-temperature aging (e.g., thermal cycling at 773–1173 K for catalytic applications or 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications) under different atmospheres (inert vs. mild oxidizing conditions) to isolate the role of surface oxidation and atomic diffusion.
generation.conditions: Service-like temperatures as stated with controlled oxygen partial pressures (ranging from inert/argon to low oxygen environments) to mimic catalytic operation or thermoelectric use.
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale evolution of the particle, specifically the onset of phase segregation and/or the formation and growth of a surface oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles facilitates accelerated atomic diffusion. Differences in atomic size and redox potentials among constituent elements lead to differential mobilities and oxidation tendencies. When the driving force for segregation (or oxidation) overcomes the entropy stabilization, the originally homogeneous, single-phase structure decomposes into regions enriched in specific elements or develops surface oxide patches, thereby degrading the designed properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that preserve a uniform elemental distribution (as verified by in situ XRD and XAS measurements) should maintain catalytic and thermoelectric performance. In contrast, samples exhibiting phase segregation or surface oxide formation will show altered diffraction patterns, changes in surface composition profiles, and degraded performance compared to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles aged at lower temperatures or under fully inert atmospheres where minimal atomic diffusion and oxidation occur, thereby maintaining their initial homogeneous structure and properties.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for service conditions up to the stated temperature ranges. At temperatures significantly above these limits (e.g., causing melting or sintering) or under extreme oxidative environments, additional degradation pathways may dominate and invalidate the predicted mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The exact contributions of individual element diffusivities and oxidation kinetics are not fully quantified. Uncertainty remains as to the relative weight of atomic size mismatch versus redox potential differences in driving segregation, and these effects may vary with the specific element set used.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles with identical initial single-phase structures. Subject one set to high-temperature aging under a mildly oxidizing atmosphere and the other under a strictly inert atmosphere. In situ XRD and multi-edge XAS will be performed during aging to monitor any changes in phase structure and surface composition. Additionally, ex situ microscopy and atom probe tomography will be used after aging. Compare catalytic or thermoelectric performance of both sets.
measurements: In situ X-ray powder diffraction (to monitor phase changes and potential segregation)
X-ray absorption spectroscopy at multiple element-specific edges (to detect oxidation states and surface composition changes)
Atom probe tomography or TEM (to resolve nanoscale chemical distribution)
Performance metrics specific to catalytic activity or thermoelectric efficiency
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the oxidizing and inert atmosphere samples exhibit equivalent preservation of the homogeneous single-phase structure, and if there is no correlation between structural changes (e.g., detected phase segregation or surface oxidation) and degradation in performance, then the proposed mechanism (i.e., that selective atomic diffusion/oxidation driven by atomic size and redox disparities is responsible for service-induced instability) is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Combined experimental and theoretical studies that utilize the predictions from computational screenings are still scarce and mainly focus on thin film catalyst materials prepared by magnetron sputtering that can be more easily performed in experimental high throughput screening studies. To be able to predict and simulate the variety of binding sites of the different elements present in a HEA, single-phase materials are crucial. If phase segregation occurs, the surface atoms are not randomly distributed anymore and the key assumption of the computational modeling is not valid. Thus the experimental and computational trends will diverge.
HEAs are conventionally prepared as bulk materials employing high-temperature methods such as arc melting. Bulk materials have very low dispersion, i.e., a low ratio of surface to bulk atoms. A large surface-to-bulk atom ratio is, however, vital for efficient catalysts. Nanoparticles possess such high dispersion. This generates a large interest in developing HEA nanoparticle synthesis methods. Many synthesis methods for HEA nanoparticles are high-energy shock methods such as Joule-heating, microwave heating, laser-ablation, and fast-bed pyrolysis. R

## Abstract
Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions.
